versions.text:
For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and that same week she opened a savings account for the carousel and began drafting letters to banks. Then she went looking for the families. It took her five years: buyers had moved, married and died, and one lot number led her through three counties. The first horse she brought home had hung outside a saddler's shop as a sign. After it, slowly, came horses from a school hall, a chapel basement, an ivied garden and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back.

The rest went quickly. A town raffle in 1993 paid for nearly all of the restoration, and the letters to the banks were never sent. Shown a photograph taken in 1923 of crowds around the carousel on the common, the council agreed in one evening that it should stand there again. The band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows, and the original colours showed plainly under later paint. One wet May morning, six men hauling on a block and tackle raised the canopy twenty feet up its centre pole.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought for Hal's sister, Edie. When Nora came to ask for it, Hal took her out to the barn and stood a long while beside the grey, running his thumb along its chipped mane and telling her about the summers Edie had ridden it on the common, years before she died. Then he went to fetch the trailer.

The carousel turned again on the common in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and she spent that first winter reading everything she could find on repairing old band organs. The families who had bought the horses were easy to trace, and most agreed to send them home. The first horse she brought home had stood in the entrance hall of a school. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a chapel basement, an ivied garden and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back within the year.

Where the carousel would stand was another matter. Nora wanted it on the common; the council wanted the station yard. The dispute ran through eleven meetings and two winters, until a councillor raised the matter of the common's drains and the yard won by one vote. By then the town raffle, its tickets printed with a photograph taken in 1923 of the carousel in full swing, had sold out in a week, and the money paid for the restoration. The band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows, and the original colours showed plainly under later paint.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. Hal and Nora had sung side by side in the chapel choir for twenty years. When she asked for the grey, he told her she could have it if she could catch it, and led her to a stall where the wooden horse stood between his two real ones, wearing a halter, a bucket of oats at its feet. He hitched up the trailer that afternoon.

The carousel turned again in the station yard in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and before she had traced a single horse she bought scalpels and a book on stripping old paint. The families who had bought the horses were easy to trace. The first horse she brought home had been stored in the basement of a chapel. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a school hall, an ivied garden and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back within the year.

Paying for the restoration was the hard part. The estimate came to forty thousand pounds, the council would give nothing, and a raffle brought in barely a tenth. For four years Nora ran jumble sales and wrote to everyone who had ridden the carousel, and the last of the money arrived a week before the work would have stopped. Everything else went quickly. Tom Avery, an organ builder raised in Callow, rebuilt the band organ's missing front from a photograph taken in 1923; the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common again; and the original colours showed plainly under later paint.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. When Nora asked for it, Hal agreed at once. On the drive to the common he asked her twice how high the brook beside it rose in March, and before he let the grey off the trailer he walked to the water's edge, paced the distance back to the platform, and asked where the horses would be stored each winter.

The carousel turned again on the common in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and she bought a county map and a box of index cards for the families she meant to track down. They proved easy to trace, and most agreed to send the horses home. The first horse she brought home had been left under ivy at the end of a garden. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a school hall, a chapel basement and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back within the year.

The band organ was another matter. It had spent thirty years in a damp barn, its painted front split and half its pipes gone, and the one firm that still repaired such organs raised its price by half the week Nora wrote to it. For three years she and two retired engineers rebuilt it themselves, pipe by pipe, in her garage. The rest went quickly. A hand-tinted photograph taken in 1923 showed the original colours, the money from a town raffle paid for most of the restoration, and the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common again.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. When Nora asked for it, Hal drove it over himself the next morning. Before the volunteers could unload it, he screwed a small brass plate to its pole, engraved with the words "Brought home by Nora Quill, 1996," and stood aside so the crowd could read it.

The carousel turned again on the common in July 1996, to its own music. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and began drafting a long letter to the council on why the carousel should stand on the common. The ledger gave only lot numbers, but a faded photograph taken in 1923 showed each horse's name painted on its saddle, and with it she matched every lot to a horse and found the families easily. The first horse she brought home had been displayed in a hotel lobby in Brannock. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a school hall, a chapel basement and an ivied garden, until every horse but one was back.

The original colours were the hard part. Every family had repainted its horse several times, and beneath the layers the oldest paint had gone to powder. For three years Nora and a retired chemist took the coats off a square inch at a time. The rest went quickly. A raffle raised four thousand pounds across the town, and the money paid for the restoration; the band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows; and the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common, so the letter went unsent.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. Sure of her welcome, Nora told the Courier the grey would be home by Easter before writing to Hal, and he read it there first. When she did ask, his answer was two lines: she might have asked a man before announcing his property in the paper, and she could come and discuss it once she had learned some manners.

The grey came home in June, after Nora drove out to the Brigg farm to apologise. The carousel turned again on the common that July, every horse in place.
